chunks: Verily, those who swore allegiance to Abū Bakr, ‘Umar and ‘Umān
have sworn allegiance [1] to me on the same basis on which they swore allegiance to them. (On this basis) he who was present has no choice (to consider), and he who was absent has no right to reject;
and consultation is confined to the muhājirūn and the anṣār.
If they agree on an individual and take him to be Caliph it will be deemed to mean Allāh’s pleasure.
If any one keeps away by way of objection or innovation they will return him to the position from where he kept away.
If he refuses they will fight him for following a course other than that of the believers
and Allāh will put him back from where he had run away.
ai.seo_question: What is Imam Ali's view on the legitimacy of the first three Caliphs and the rights of the Muhajirun and Ansar in governance?
ai.summary: In this letter to Muawiya, Imam ‘Alī (peace be upon him) asserts the continuity of political legitimacy by linking his caliphate to the precedent of the first three Caliphs, arguing that the initial pledge (bay‘ah) by the Muhājirūn and Anṣār binds all subsequent generations. He clarifies that the authority of shūrā (consultation) was specific to the founding companions, thereby establishing their selection as divinely accepted (ridā Allāh) and creating a binding consensus for the community. The passage concludes with a theological justification for the civil wars against dissenters, framing their rebellion not merely as political opposition but as a deviation from the established path of the believers.
